definition: A model's ability to maintain reliable performance when faced with noisy, out-of-distribution, or adversarially perturbed inputs.
details: Robustness is a key concern for deploying models in real-world settings, where inputs will inevitably differ from the clean, curated data seen during training and evaluation.

explainer.lead: Robustness is how well a model keeps performing when inputs are noisy, unlike its training data, or deliberately tampered with. Without it, results on clean test sets can overstate what a deployed system will actually do.

tiers.eli5: It's like a recipe that still turns out fine when you're missing an ingredient or the oven runs a bit hot, instead of only working under perfect conditions.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers stress-test models with noise, distribution shifts, and adversarial examples before deployment, and often train on perturbed data to harden them. A common pitfall is assuming strong benchmark accuracy carries over to messy real-world inputs.
tiers.paperLevel: Formally, robustness is the model's maintained performance under inputs drawn from noise, distribution shift, or adversarial perturbation rather than the clean training distribution; how much performance degrades is not fixed and depends on the type and strength of perturbation.

explainer.example: A classifier scores 95% on a clean test set but drops sharply when images are blurred or slightly altered, showing low robustness.
